title: Reading a Crash: Finding Your Own Frame

questions.question: A backtrace shows nine frames, eight of them inside /usr/include. Where do you look first?
options: Frame zero, since that is where it stopped
Whichever frame mentions your function name
The last frame, which is always main
The first frame in a file you wrote, however far down it is
questions.explanation: Library frames are almost always where a correct library reacted to something you handed it. Starting at frame zero here means reading the standard library for an hour.

questions.question: What does frame zero represent?
options: Where execution was when it stopped
The function that allocated the memory
The oldest frame on the stack
Where the program started
questions.explanation: Frames run most recent first. Frame one called frame zero, and so on outward to main.

questions.question: What is the difference between a debugger backtrace and a sanitizer one?
options: The debugger has no line numbers
They are completely different formats
The sanitizer numbers its frames backwards
The debugger writes at before the file, the sanitizer puts the location last
questions.explanation: Both give an index, an address, a function after the word in, and a file with a line. That near identity is why one small parser handles both.

questions.question: A heap buffer overflow crashes inside std::sort. What is the most likely cause?
options: The elements are not copyable
The comparator is not a strict weak ordering
A bug in the standard library
The vector was too small to sort
questions.explanation: The sort runs off the end. A comparator that reports an element as less than itself makes the sort look for a pivot that cannot exist. The crash is in the library and the defect is in the argument.

questions.question: Why does the reference keep frames that have no file or line?
options: So the frame count matches the stack depth exactly
Because the parser cannot tell whether a file is missing
Dropping them would renumber everything after and make the report harder to follow
Because they are often the cause
questions.explanation: A frame with no debug information still occupies a position. Keeping it preserves the correspondence with what the tool printed.

questions.question: Why check for a use after free before checking for an overflow?
options: A use after free report also names a heap address
Because use after free is more serious
The order does not matter
Because overflows never mention addresses
questions.explanation: An overflow check would match it first. Classification by substring has to run most specific first, which is a general rule for this kind of matching rather than a quirk of these two.
